description: Guidance data for Step 8 Risk Assessment. Edit this file to adapt the language, categories, applies-if conditions, and relevance rules to suit your organisation. This file is loaded at runtime by step8-wizard.js — no code changes are required.

Human Control.description: Risks that arise when AI systems act without adequate human oversight, intervention capability, or explainability.

Bias & Fairness.description: Risks that AI systems produce outcomes that are systematically unfair or discriminatory toward identifiable groups.

Data Integrity.description: Risks arising from poor quality, undocumented, or improperly governed training and input data.

Monitoring & Audit.description: Risks that AI decisions cannot be traced, audited, or reconstructed due to inadequate logging.

Cybersecurity.description: Risks from adversarial attacks, model manipulation, and unauthorised extraction of model logic or data.

Access Control.description: Risks arising from insufficient identity management, privilege controls, or access governance over AI systems and their data.

Performance Integrity.description: Risks that AI accuracy, reliability, or reproducibility degrades in production without detection.

Availability & Resilience.description: Risks that AI system failures are not handled safely, causing operational disruption or harm.

Transparency.description: Risks arising from failure to disclose AI involvement, AI-generated content, or AI-driven decisions to affected parties.

Infrastructure Security.description: Risks to the AI deployment environment: containers, registries, network exposure, and host isolation.

relevance_factor_keys.high_if_step3_ai_act_outcome: HIGH if Step 3 AI Act classification is one of the listed outcomes
relevance_factor_keys.high_if_step7_automated_decisions_contai: HIGH if Step 7 automated decision-making answer contains any of the listed substrings
relevance_factor_keys.high_if_step7_has_special_categories: HIGH if Step 7 DPIA identified any special-category data (GDPR Art.9)
relevance_factor_keys.high_if_step7_has_personal_data: HIGH if Step 7 DPIA identified any standard personal data
relevance_factor_keys.high_if_step7_training_data_used: HIGH if Step 7 DPIA indicates personal data is or may be used to train/fine-tune the model

Human Oversight Bypass Failure.traditional_analog: Automation over-reliance — like unchecked automated trading or credit-scoring systems with no kill switch or mandatory human review checkpoint before consequential action is taken.
applies_if: AI output is used to make or significantly influence decisions without a mandatory human review step
Users have no mechanism to override, halt, or contest AI-driven actions
The AI system provides no confidence indicator or explanation alongside its outputs

Subgroup Coverage Failure.traditional_analog: Sampling bias in analytics — like an underrepresented demographic in credit-scoring training data, where sparse records cause systematically worse outcomes for that group at inference time.
applies_if: The AI system processes data about or makes decisions that affect distinct groups of people (by age, gender, ethnicity, disability, or other protected characteristic)
Training data was collected over a period or from a source where certain groups may have been underrepresented
The AI system's outputs affect employment, credit, benefits, healthcare access, or other individually significant decisions

Proxy Discrimination Propagation Failure.traditional_analog: Redlining / indirect discrimination — where a seemingly neutral variable (e.g. postcode, browsing history) acts as a statistical proxy for a protected characteristic, producing discriminatory outcomes that are harder to detect than direct discrimination.
applies_if: The AI uses data variables that may correlate with protected characteristics (e.g. location, purchasing patterns, social connections)
The AI ranks, scores, or filters individuals for employment, credit, insurance, benefits, or similar consequential decisions
Historical decisions are used as training labels and may embed past discriminatory patterns

Dataset Lifecycle Integrity Failure.traditional_analog: Database change management failure — like a version-controlled ETL pipeline where an undocumented schema change silently corrupts downstream analytical models, discovered only during an audit.
applies_if: The AI model is periodically retrained or fine-tuned on updated data
The system's knowledge base (RAG pipeline) is refreshed with new documents or data feeds
Third-party or externally sourced datasets are ingested without formal versioning and validation

Data Governance Documentation Failure.traditional_analog: Undocumented data lineage / missing information asset register — like an ETL pipeline with no data dictionary, where no one can trace the origin, transformation logic, or quality of data feeding a regulatory report.
applies_if: The AI system uses training data that must be documented to satisfy regulatory or legal obligations
Data lineage traceability is required for audit, legal proceedings, or GDPR Article 30 records
Multiple data sources are combined and their provenance and quality must be tracked and evidenced

Data Quality Measurement Failure.traditional_analog: Silent data quality degradation in production — like a financial reporting system that passes incomplete or duplicate records through an ETL pipeline with no quality checks, producing incorrect regulatory submissions.
applies_if: The AI system's outputs depend directly on the quality and completeness of input data
No formal data quality metrics, thresholds, or validation rules are applied before data is used
Errors in input data would propagate into AI-driven decisions without triggering an alert or rejection

Audit Log Integrity Failure.traditional_analog: SOX / GDPR audit trail tampering — like a financial transaction log that can be modified or deleted, making post-incident investigation and regulatory audit impossible and creating legal exposure.
applies_if: The AI system is subject to regulatory logging requirements (GDPR Art.22, EU AI Act Art.12, internal compliance policy)
Audit trails are required to reconstruct or justify AI decisions in the event of a complaint, legal challenge, or regulatory review
AI decision logs are stored in a system where they could be modified, deleted, or are not protected from tampering

Log Retention Violation.traditional_analog: Log retention policy breach / evidence spoliation — like security event logs deleted before the mandatory retention window, preventing forensic investigation after an incident and creating regulatory exposure.
applies_if: The AI system's operational logs are subject to a defined minimum retention period (regulatory, contractual, or internal policy)
Logs are stored in systems with automatic deletion, rolling overwrite, or size-based truncation that could violate retention requirements
Historical AI decision logs may be required for regulatory audit, data subject requests, or post-incident investigation

Adversarial Input Evasion Failure.traditional_analog: Input validation bypass / AI-layer SQL injection — where a malicious user crafts inputs designed to manipulate the model's logic or extract sensitive information, analogous to how SQL injection exploits improperly sanitised database queries.
applies_if: The AI system accepts natural language or structured input directly from users (prompt injection risk)
The system is exposed to potentially adversarial, untrusted, or external users or data sources
Security controls rely on the AI model itself to detect and reject malicious inputs rather than a separate validation layer

Model Extraction Attack Failure.traditional_analog: Intellectual property theft via API probing — like systematically querying a competitor's pricing or credit-scoring API to reverse-engineer and replicate their proprietary algorithm without authorisation.
applies_if: The AI model embodies commercially valuable, proprietary, or competitively sensitive decision logic
The model is accessible via an API, web interface, or other queryable endpoint that could be systematically interrogated
Replication of the model's behaviour by a competitor, adversary, or data subject would cause commercial or reputational harm

Development Environment Integrity Failur.traditional_analog: Software supply chain attack (SolarWinds-style) — where a compromised development environment or third-party library injects malicious code or biased data into the AI model before it reaches production.
applies_if: The AI model is built, fine-tuned, or customised in-house using an internal development or training pipeline
Third-party libraries, pre-trained foundation models, or external data sources are incorporated into the AI build
The development or CI/CD pipeline has access to sensitive systems, credentials, or production data

Unauthorised Access and Privilege Escala.traditional_analog: Privileged access management (PAM) failure / RBAC violation — like a compromised service account with excessive permissions giving an attacker access to sensitive model weights, training data, or the AI decision pipeline.
applies_if: The AI system stores sensitive data (training data, personal data, model weights, inference logs) requiring formal access controls
Multiple users, teams, or automated systems have access to the AI infrastructure with different privilege levels
Access to the AI model, its data, or its configuration is not governed by a documented and enforced IAM policy

Cyber Attack Detection Failure.traditional_analog: IDS/SIEM gap — like a web server silently exfiltrating sensitive data for weeks because anomalous query patterns were not monitored, leaving the organisation without early warning of an active attack.
applies_if: The AI system processes sensitive or personal data that could be targeted for exfiltration via query manipulation
Prompt injection or adversarial inputs could manipulate AI outputs to bypass controls or leak information
No automated monitoring exists to detect unusual query volumes, anomalous output patterns, or potential AI-layer attacks

Accuracy Measurement and Drift Failure.traditional_analog: Model drift / SLA degradation in production — like a fraud detection model that was 95% accurate at launch but silently degraded to 70% over 18 months as fraud patterns changed, with no monitoring alert to trigger retraining.
applies_if: The AI system makes consequential decisions that depend on maintaining a defined level of accuracy or performance
The system is deployed in an environment where the characteristics of input data may evolve over time
No baseline accuracy metric, monitoring threshold, or automated drift detection alert has been defined

Feedback Loop Contamination Failure.traditional_analog: Self-reinforcing algorithmic error — like a recommendation engine trained on user clicks that progressively amplifies engagement-optimising content, embedding and amplifying its own biases with each retraining cycle.
applies_if: The AI system learns from, adapts to, or is retrained using user interactions, feedback, or behavioural signals
The system is periodically retrained on data that includes outputs previously generated by the AI itself
Errors or biases in current AI outputs could become embedded as ground truth in future training data

Output Reproducibility Failure.traditional_analog: Audit reproducibility requirement — like a regulatory capital model that cannot reproduce a prior month's output because an undocumented parameter was changed, making supervisory review and model validation impossible.
applies_if: AI-generated outputs must be reproducible for regulatory audit, legal proceedings, or compliance review
Identical or equivalent inputs should produce consistent results for legal, contractual, or risk management reasons
Post-incident investigation requires the ability to reconstruct and replay a specific AI decision or output

Input Corruption Propagation Failure.traditional_analog: Garbage-in-garbage-out / upstream data quality cascade — like a risk model silently ingesting corrupted market data feeds and producing incorrect risk calculations for hours before detection, with no validation gate between ingest and processing.
applies_if: The AI system ingests real-time or externally sourced data feeds that could be corrupted, incomplete, or manipulated
No validation or sanity-check gate exists between data ingestion and AI processing
Corrupted or anomalous inputs would propagate directly into AI outputs without triggering an alert or rejection

Fail-Safe Activation Failure.traditional_analog: Circuit breaker / graceful degradation failure — like a critical payment processing system with no fallback mode, where a software fault causes total service loss rather than a safe degraded state or manual override.
applies_if: The AI system is relied upon for time-sensitive or operationally critical functions where failure causes direct harm
A system fault would leave users, staff, or affected individuals without a safe fallback or manual alternative
No defined safe-state, limited-functionality mode, or emergency halt mechanism has been designed and tested

AI Disclosure Mechanism Failure.traditional_analog: Consumer protection / advertising standards non-disclosure — like undisclosed AI-generated product reviews or a chatbot that does not identify itself as AI, violating EU AI Act Art.50 and consumer protection law transparency obligations.
applies_if: The AI system interacts directly with members of the public, customers, or employees in a way that could be mistaken for human interaction
AI-generated content is published, distributed, or used to inform decisions without labelling or attribution
The EU AI Act Art.50 transparency obligations apply to this system's output or interaction modality

Image Integrity & Supply Chain Failure.traditional_analog: Software supply chain attack (dependency confusion / typosquatting) — like a malicious npm package injecting credential-stealing code during a CI/CD build, or a tampered Docker base image silently adding a backdoor to the production system.
applies_if: The AI system is deployed as a containerised application and base images or model artefacts are pulled from public or shared registries
The CI/CD pipeline does not verify the integrity (cryptographic hash or signature) of all dependencies before build
Model artefacts or weights are downloaded from external sources (e.g. HuggingFace) without hash verification

Registry & Identity Access Failure.traditional_analog: Service account credential theft / registry access control failure — like a compromised CI/CD service account allowing an attacker to push malicious images to a private container registry, silently replacing production workloads.
applies_if: The AI deployment uses a container or model registry authenticated via service accounts, API keys, or machine credentials
Multiple teams or automated pipelines share access to the deployment infrastructure with potentially overlapping permissions
A compromised credential would allow an attacker to modify, replace, or exfiltrate AI model artefacts

Network Exposure & API Abuse Failure.traditional_analog: Exposed API endpoint / network segmentation failure — like an internal administrative API accidentally exposed to the internet, allowing unauthorised query submission, data extraction, or resource exhaustion via automated probing.
applies_if: The AI system is accessible via an API endpoint, whether internal or external-facing
Network access controls are required to restrict which users or systems can query the AI model
High or unlimited query volumes could be used to extract model behaviour, exhaust resources, or perform denial-of-service attacks

Host & Workload Isolation Failure.traditional_analog: VM escape / container breakout in shared cloud — like a malicious workload in a shared cloud environment exploiting a hypervisor vulnerability to access memory or storage belonging to a co-located sensitive AI workload.
applies_if: The AI system runs in a shared or multi-tenant infrastructure environment (public cloud, co-located data centre, shared Kubernetes cluster)
Sensitive training data, model weights, or inference outputs could be exposed if workload isolation fails
The AI system processes personal or sensitive data in an environment shared with other workloads of varying trust levels

Container Runtime Security Failure.traditional_analog: RASP gap / container running as root — like a containerised application with no runtime monitoring and elevated privileges, where an attacker who gains code execution has unrestricted access to the host and adjacent workloads.
applies_if: The AI system is deployed in containers that require runtime security controls and behavioural monitoring
Containers run with elevated privileges or with access to sensitive host resources (volumes, network namespaces)
No runtime anomaly detection exists to identify compromised container behaviour, unusual process execution, or lateral movement

wizard_questions.question: Does the AI system make or significantly influence decisions without a mandatory human review or override step?
Does the AI system process data about, or make decisions that affect, people from distinct demographic or protected groups (age, gender, ethnicity, disability, etc.)?
Does the AI use input variables — such as location, purchasing history, or social network data — that could act as proxies for protected characteristics?
Are formal controls in place governing the collection, labelling, versioning, and retirement of all training datasets?
Is the data lineage, schema, and quality thresholds for all training data formally documented and maintained?
Is the quality, completeness, and representativeness of training data regularly measured and reported against defined thresholds?
Does the AI system generate comprehensive, tamper-evident audit logs of its decisions, inputs, and actions?
Are AI system logs retained for the full period required by applicable regulations, internal policies, or contractual obligations?
Does the AI system accept external or user-supplied inputs that directly influence its predictions or decisions?
Is the trained model or its outputs exposed through APIs or interfaces accessible to users or systems outside your organisation?
Are the development and training pipelines protected against supply-chain attacks or unauthorised injection of code or data?
Does the AI system have monitoring controls to detect anomalous query patterns, unusual output behaviour, or attempted intrusions?

wizard_questions.risk_name: Unauthorised Access and Privilege Escalation Failure
wizard_questions.question: Are role-based access controls in place limiting who can query, modify, retrain, or administer the AI system?
Is the AI system's accuracy formally measured at deployment and monitored on an ongoing basis for model drift or degradation?
Does the AI system use its own historical outputs — directly or indirectly — as future training or reinforcement data?
Is reproducibility required for this system — must the same input reliably produce the same output across runs and environments?
Could corrupted, spoofed, or low-quality data reach the model without detection by an upstream validation or anomaly-detection layer?
Is a fail-safe or fallback mode defined and tested for when the AI system becomes unavailable or produces outputs below an acceptable confidence threshold?
Are users or individuals affected by the system's outputs notified that they are interacting with, or being assessed by, an AI system?
Are container images and model artefacts cryptographically signed or verified for integrity before deployment?
Are container or model registries protected with access controls, authentication, and audit logging?
Are AI system APIs and service endpoints protected against unauthorised external access, rate abuse, and data exfiltration?
Are AI workloads isolated from other systems at the host, VM, or container level to prevent lateral movement in the event of a compromise?
Are container runtime security controls applied — such as read-only filesystems, dropped capabilities, non-root execution, and syscall filtering?
